title: A vote rule that compares log length before term grants a vote it must refuse
summary: The election model checks the vote rule's decision kernel, generated from its contract, and repeats the arithmetic around it: how the candidate's term and log compare with the voter's own is computed in `grant`, outside the model's reach. A developer reorders that comparison so that the longer log wins and the term of the last entry breaks ties between logs of one length, reading "up to date" as "further along". The kernel's contract does not change and the election model verifies it under every configuration, logs included, since the model does its own comparing. The property that states the election restriction over `grant` itself, that a candidate whose last entry is of an older term is refused however long its log, fails: JBMC shows a voter whose last entry is of a later term granting a candidate whose log is longer but ends in an earlier one, the log a deposed leader left behind. Example 013 catches the same rewrite as a regression against the previous version of the method; this one needs no previous version, only the rule.

change.description: Compare the last indices first, and the last terms only between logs of the same length, with a comment: the longer log is the one further along, and between logs of one length the one with the newer last entry. The comparisons are the same two; only their order changes, and a longer log being further along reads as what "up to date" means. No test changes: the tests compare logs of one term, or one length.

risk: The order of the two comparisons is the election restriction. A log is a sequence of entries with terms, and the term of the last entry says which leader wrote it last: a log that ends in term 2 was matched to the leader of term 2, a longer log that ends in term 1 was left behind when term 1's leader was deposed, with entries no later leader ever confirmed. Rank by length and the server left behind outranks the servers that have the committed entries, wins the election with their votes, and overwrites those entries with its own. The existing tests pass: they compare logs of one term, where length decides either way, or of one length, where the term decides either way. The reviewer sees two comparisons swapped under a comment that reads correctly, in a method whose decision kernel and contract are untouched; the election model, which the module's other checks run, verifies the change in every configuration, because it computes the comparison itself and hands the result to the kernel.
explanation: JBMC proves each property of `VoteRule#grant` over every input, the eight parameters ranging over their whole types. The property that states the election restriction, that a candidate whose last entry is of an older term than the voter's is refused however long its log, and between equal last terms the shorter log is, fails on the patched comparison, and JBMC gives the input: a voter with an open ballot whose last entry is of a later term than the candidate's, and a candidate with a longer log, for which `grant` returns true. The other two properties, one vote per term and no vote for a candidate from the past, still hold. The model would not have found this: the comparison lives in `grant`, which the model repeats in TLA+ rather than generates, so a change to it changes the Java and not the model. The kernel's contract is the boundary, and this change stays on the far side of it. That is what the properties are for, and why the module runs both. Example 013 is the same rewrite proved not equivalent to the version before it, which needs that version; a property states what the rule must do and holds the method to it whatever it replaced.
resolution: Restore the order: the term of the last entry first, and length only between equal terms, as section 5.4.1 of the paper defines "up to date". Then add the test the suite lacks, a longer log that ends in an older term against a shorter one that ends in a newer. The split between the kernel and the arithmetic is the module's design, and each half has its check: the contract and the model for the decisions, the properties for the comparisons that feed them.
notes: The Raft election model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla`) is built around the role machine, generated from its contract, with election safety as an invariant and two action properties, `[][A]_v` formulas that constrain each step: terms never decrease, a leader never campaigns. An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.

The model repeats the arithmetic around the vote rule rather than generating it, so it cannot see this change; the property proofs of `VoteRule#grant` can. Compare 069 and 070, the model-checked changes to the same rule.

JBMC's own gaps (step 4c of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, job 20261106-082917, JDK 25.0.4.1, under `--gaps assume`): each of the three properties' proofs reaches `jdk-constructor:java.lang.Enum.<init>(Ljava/lang/String;I)V`, `jdk-static-method:java.util.List.copyOf(Ljava/util/Collection;)Ljava/util/List;` and `jdk-static-method:java.util.List.of([Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/util/List;`, which JBMC stubs (no bytecode on its class path). Under strict, the first two properties, established under assume, would be no verdict; the third, refuted, stands, so the example's verdict, a violation, does not move. Contracts for the three calls under `--gaps advised` would let the two proofs stand. With 013, the only recorded JBMC examples that reach a JBMC gap.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 7 November 2026, JDK 25.0.5, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets 2 gaps in what the proof reaches: `jdk-static-method:java.util.List.copyOf(Ljava/util/Collection;)Ljava/util/List;@jdk-25.0.5` (first at net.terminalvalue.quorum.Decision$Transition.<init>:18); `jdk-static-method:java.util.List.of([Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/util/List;@jdk-25.0.5` (first at net.terminalvalue.quorum.Decision.transition:30). Under strict mode each is refused by name, and a run by the tool's own checker would end with no verdict; the example runs in `assume` until the user decides how the recorded examples move. A `jdk-static-method` gap has no assume form: `assume` refuses it too, and only a contract closes it (`--gaps advised`). The recorded proof is JBMC's, which strict mode of the tool's own checker does not change. JBMC's own approximations are step 4c's.

Phase 5 of `llm-dlc/loops/engine-priorities.md`, under strict, JDK 25.0.5, on JBMC: job 20261106-203501 left the first two properties' proofs no verdict on two stubs, `Collection.isEmpty` and `toArray`, which JBMC's call graph reaches in the model of `List.copyOf` (`Enum.<init>`, `List.of` and `List.copyOf` are models on JBMC's class path now, no gaps). Job 20261107-012013 named the two stubs as never entered by JBMC's symbolic execution of the proof, so no gaps, but left the two proofs no verdict on two `extra-initializer` defects, at `VoteRule.decide:39` and `grant:63`, that JBMC does not have: the preflight read JBMC's goto listing by bytecode offset where the listing numbers instructions by their place in the method, and at offset 12 (`invokestatic Decision.rejected`) it read index 12, `getstatic Ballot.FOR_ANOTHER`. Read by index, none of the three proofs reaches a defect (checked on that job's listings). The third property's violation, replayed, stood in both jobs. Rerun as job 20261107-024759.

Job 20261107-024759 (at 854a0d8f, vm-1, JDK 25.0.5) passed, and this result is its run: under `--gaps strict` on JBMC, the first two properties are verified with no gap, the stubs `Collection.isEmpty` and `Collection.toArray` named as reached by the call graph and never entered by the proof's symbolic execution, and the third property's violation replays. With the preflight reading JBMC's listing by instruction index, no `extra-initializer` defect is named. That closes VF-005 and Phase 5's last criterion.
provenance: Constructed from the definition of "up to date" in section 5.4.1 of the paper, inverted, which is the bug the paper's wording guards against.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (2014): section 5.2, leader election, and section 5.4.1, the election restriction
